position: Chapter author's recommendation; the chapter notes some conservatives (including contributors) oppose regulating private platforms' content moderation on First Amendment grounds (p. 850).
proposal: The FCC should issue an order reading Section 230 so that platforms do not get broad immunity for moderation decisions beyond the statute's text, treating the narrower good-faith provision as the one that covers restricting others' content. It should also adopt transparency rules for large platforms modeled on broadband disclosure rules, with clearer terms of service and an appeals process, and work with Congress on further reform.

FCC transparency and appeals rules for large online platforms, with an identified legal basis
Legislation reforming Section 230 in the way the chapter describes (the pending Sunset Section 230 Act would repeal rather than narrow it)

status_summary: No FCC order interpreting Section 230 and no FCC transparency or appeals rules for large online platforms were found as of 2026-10-16. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, the author of the chapter, said on 2025-02-27 that it is appropriate for the FCC to take another look at Section 230, but no notice, petition, declaratory ruling or docket on the subject was found. Federal Register queries for FCC documents published since 2025-01-20 returned no results for Section 230, content moderation, Big Tech or interactive computer service, and a query for social media returned twelve FCC documents, none about platform moderation or Section 230; a query across all agencies for Section 230 returned five documents, none from the FCC. Congress has moved on the legislative side of the topic: a bipartisan Senate bill to repeal Section 230 two years after enactment (the Sunset Section 230 Act) was introduced on 2025-12-17 as S. 3546 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and the Senate Commerce Committee held a hearing titled 'Liability or Deniability? Platform Power as Section 230 Turns 30' on 2026-03-18; neither involves an FCC order or rule. Two House bills, H.R. 6746 (introduced 2025-12-16, a sunset of Section 230) and H.R. 10332 (introduced 2026-09-10, a repeal), were referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and show no later action, and the FCC's entries in the current Unified Agenda (Fall 2025) include no Section 230 or platform item. As of the 2026-10-16 check, the GovInfo bill status for S. 3546 showed no action after referral, and the FCC's own document system could not be searched, so non-Federal Register FCC items cannot be ruled out.

timeline.event: At a public event in Washington, FCC Chairman Carr says it is appropriate for the FCC to take another look at Section 230 and that he is eager to apply the law as Congress passed it; Reason's report of 2025-02-28 describes no formal FCC proceeding, order or docket and notes critics' view that, after Loper Bright (2024), the FCC lacks authority to reinterpret the statute.

Representative Hageman introduces the Sunset To Reform Section 230 Act (H.R. 6746), which would set a sunset for Section 230; referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the same day, with no later action in the GovInfo bill status. This is a congressional bill, not an FCC action.

Senator Graham introduces the Sunset Section 230 Act (S. 3546), a bill to repeal Section 230 of the Communications Act; per GovInfo bill status it was read twice and referred to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee the same day, and a bipartisan Senate Judiciary Committee release of 2025-12-18 describes it as repealing the provision two years after enactment. This is a congressional bill, not an FCC action, and it repeals the provision rather than reading it narrowly as the chapter proposes.
H.R. 7045, the PROTECT Act, a bill to repeal Section 230 of the Communications Act, is introduced in the House and referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee.

The Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee holds a hearing titled 'Liability or Deniability? Platform Power as Section 230 Turns 30'; a local public radio report of 2026-03-25 says the Sunset Section 230 Act (S. 3546) had not come up for a vote and does not mention the FCC.

Representative DeSaulnier introduces a House Sunset Section 230 Act (H.R. 10332), a bill to repeal Section 230; referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the same day, with no later action in the GovInfo bill status. This is a congressional bill, not an FCC action, and it repeals rather than narrows the provision.
